correctness.summary: After a length-increasing update (the 2*L<=i branch) the shift counter m is reset to 0 instead of 1. In the single-array Berlekamp-Massey, the correction polynomial b must be applied shifted by m=1 on the next discrepancy, because b was captured BEFORE this iteration's term. Resetting to 0 misaligns the index j+m in UpdateCoefficients, producing a wrong (and over-long) connection polynomial and an inflated reported length L+1. Verified against a reference BM on 500 random LFSR sequences: every case mismatched with m=0, and every case matched after changing to m=1.
correctness.triggeringInput: s = sequence generated by a degree-4 LFSR over MOD=998244353, e.g. the first 20 terms of any order-4 recurrence; the routine returns L=10 with trailing-zero / incorrect coefficients instead of the true minimal recurrence of length 4.
correctness.rootCause: Line 47: `m = 0;` in the 2*L<=i branch. The classic algorithm keeps m as the gap since the last length change and must restart it at 1, not 0, so that the freshly stored b is applied with a one-step shift on the next non-zero discrepancy.
correctness.suggestedFix: Change line 47 from `m = 0;` to `m = 1;`. (Confirmed: with m=1 the output matches a reference BM on all 500 randomized tests.)

perf.summary: Modular reduction uses % MOD per multiply-accumulate in the two hot inner loops where a single deferred reduction or branchless correction would halve the division count.
perf.currentCost: CalculateDiscrepancy does d = (d + c[j]*s[i-j]) % MOD every j -> one 64-bit division per term. UpdateCoefficients does c[idx] = (c[idx] - (factor*b[j]) % MOD + MOD) % MOD -> two divisions per term. Divisions dominate on ARM.
perf.proposedChange: In UpdateCoefficients replace the outer (...+MOD)%MOD with branchless add-if-negative: long t = c[idx] - (factor*b[j])%MOD; c[idx] = t + ((t>>63)&MOD). In CalculateDiscrepancy, if MOD^2*L fits in long (i.e. MOD < ~2^31 and L bounded so the running sum < 2^63), accumulate without per-term % and reduce once at the end; otherwise keep per-term but drop to single % since c[j]*s[i-j] with reduced inputs < MOD^2 < 2^62 needs no intermediate correction.
perf.rationale: Deferring/eliminating the second modulo converts a 64-bit divide into a shift+and+add. CalculateDiscrepancy can batch reductions when the accumulator provably stays below 2^63, cutting L divisions down to one per discrepancy.
perf.risk: Batching in CalculateDiscrepancy requires sum of up to L terms each < MOD^2 to stay < 2^63: needs L*MOD^2 < 2^63. With int MOD ~2^31 this allows only L up to ~2, so batching is generally unsafe -- instead just guarantee c[j], s[] are pre-reduced into [0,MOD) so a single % per term suffices (the current code already keeps them reduced). The UpdateCoefficients branchless correction is always safe given factor,b[j] in [0,MOD).

perf.summary: CopyArray and InitArrays iterate to n with per-element loops; these are memcpy/memset-shaped and the CopyArray(c,tmp,n) on every nonzero discrepancy copies n+1 longs even though only indices [0..L] are meaningful.
perf.currentCost: CopyArray copies n+1 longs each call; called once per nonzero discrepancy plus once per length-increase. Since only c[0..L] are nonzero, copying the full n+1 each time is up to O(n) wasted per step -> O(n^2) total in the worst case.
perf.proposedChange: Bound the copy by the live degree: copy only L+1 (or current max degree) entries into tmp, and copy L+1 from tmp into b on the length-update branch. Track the actual populated length instead of always using n. For the bulk zero/copy of full arrays, these are vectorizable element loops Burst will SIMD, so keep the loop form but shrink the count.
perf.rationale: Reducing copy length from n+1 to L+1 cuts the per-step copy cost proportional to current recurrence length, which is typically far below n early in the scan, lowering the constant factor of the O(n^2) algorithm.
perf.risk: Must ensure b is consulted only up to its populated length in UpdateCoefficients (it iterates j<=L using the L captured at copy time) -- the b[j] for j>copied-length must be zero. Since arrays start zeroed and only [0..L] are written, copying L+1 leaves higher indices at their prior (zero) value only if they were never dirtied; safest is to copy max(prevL, L)+1. Verify against tests.
